enrichment.short_title: Adequacy of intentional homelessness review reasons
key_facts: The appellant was evicted from a flat in Kensington after rent arrears and the council decided he was intentionally homeless on review.
He relied on psychiatric evidence, including Dr Browne's addendum opinion that depression rendered him incapable of making himself intentionally homeless.
The review officer's letter of 19 July 2002 did not expressly refer to Dr Browne's report but addressed other medical evidence and the appellant's capacity around April 2000.
On a section 204 appeal, the county court judge admitted a supplemental witness statement from the review officer explaining why Dr Browne's opinion was rejected.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court decision on a point of law under section 204 Housing Act 1996.
enrichment.ratio: A homelessness review decision letter may adequately explain rejection of a psychiatric opinion even without naming every report, and a decision-maker's later statement identifying material considered and elucidating reasoning on a contemporaneous opinion does not offend Ermakov if it does not fundamentally alter the stated reasons; the council was not obliged to seek clarification of an ambiguous addendum where other medical evidence already supported the intentional homelessness finding.
legal_issues: Whether the review decision gave adequate reasons for finding intentional homelessness
Admissibility of a decision-maker's supplemental statement on a section 204 appeal
Whether the council failed to make necessary enquiries into Dr Browne's opinion
Construction of section 191 intentional homelessness

enrichment.short_title: Revocability of Jehovah's Witness advance directive
key_facts: A 24-year-old Jehovah's Witness signed an advance medical directive in 2001 refusing blood transfusion.
She became critically ill with septic shock and gangrene and was unconscious when her Muslim father applied urgently for permission to override the directive.
The father gave evidence that she had abandoned Jehovah's Witness faith by early 2003 to marry a Muslim fiancé and had said she did not want to die.
The hospital considered it could not override the directive without court intervention; the Official Solicitor acted as litigation friend.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent ex parte application in the Family Division for declaratory relief during a medical emergency, with full reasons given later.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that, notwithstanding the advance directive, blood transfusion and other treatment in the patient's best interests was lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Advance directives are inherently revocable and may be revoked orally without formalities; any clause purporting to require written revocation is void as contrary to public policy; those asserting continuing validity bear the burden of clear and convincing proof, and where life is at stake doubt must be resolved in favour of preservation of life.
legal_issues: Continuing validity of an advance medical directive where the patient lacks capacity
Formal requirements for creation and revocation of advance directives
Burden and standard of proof where refusal of treatment may be fatal
Effect of a change of religious faith on an anticipatory refusal of blood products

enrichment.short_title: Inspector's curtilage misdirection on farm workshop

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Appeals) (Written Representations Procedure) (England) Regulations 2000

key_facts: Mr Wheeler appealed against refusal of retrospective planning permission for a workshop and against an enforcement notice at Three Ways Farm in the High Weald AONB.
A separate appeal concerned variation of a condition restricting an annex to dependant-relative use for self-catering holiday letting.
The inspector held the workshop was outside the dwelling curtilage, misquoting Sinclair-Lockhart's Trustees by saying the building 'must serve' the house rather than 'it is enough' that it does so.
On the annex appeal the inspector relied on unaccompanied traffic observations at a junction after telling parties he had already inspected the access.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court challenge under section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 and application for leave to appeal under section 289(6) against an inspector's written representation decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Workshop planning and enforcement appeals succeeded and were quashed or remitted; annex appeal challenge dismissed; claimant awarded two-thirds of costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where an inspector determines a decisive curtilage issue by misstating the legal test from case law not cited by the parties, the decision cannot stand even if other factual reasoning appears in the letter; by contrast, an unaccompanied site visit fairly disclosed to the parties, with opportunity to request an accompanied visit, does not breach natural justice.

Fairness where an inspector relies on case law not raised in written representations
Natural justice and unaccompanied inspector site visits on highway safety
Appropriate costs apportionment on split success

enrichment.short_title: Validity of aspartame static crystallisation patent
key_facts: Daesang sought revocation of Ajinomoto's European patent EP 0 091 787 for industrial purification of aspartame by static cooling crystallisation.
Anticipation and obviousness were alleged over Japanese laid-open specification JP '267, which focused on ion-exchange purification rather than crystallisation method.
The patented process produced a sherbet-like pseudo-solid of bundle-like crystal aggregates with improved filterability.
Experts agreed static industrial crystallisation was counterintuitive and that JP '267 did not clearly disclose static crystallisation or pseudo-solid formation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patent revocation trial in the Patents Court on anticipation, obviousness, and insufficiency.
enrichment.outcome: Revocation claim dismissed; patent held valid.
enrichment.ratio: JP '267 does not contain clear and unmistakable directions to perform static industrial-scale aspartame crystallisation producing the claimed pseudo-solid phase; even routine laboratory work would not obviously lead a skilled team to adopt unagitated industrial crystallisation over conventional agitated systems given common general knowledge and the unexpected nature of the pseudo-solid.
legal_issues: Whether JP '267 anticipates claim 1 of EP 0 091 787
Obviousness over JP '267 and common general knowledge
Construction of 'industrial scale' and pseudo-solid claim features
Insufficiency and ambiguity of bundle-like crystal aggregates

confidence.notes: Validity conclusion and detailed prior art analysis are explicit; no infringement issue was tried.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of Law Society SDT referral
key_facts: The claimant solicitor challenged Law Society panel decisions referring allegations of practising in breach of conditions and failing to notify bankruptcy to the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal.
He alleged procedural unfairness, including that a Saunders statement may not have been before the panel on the breach-of-conditions allegation.
A single judge had already refused leave, noting the SDT had certified a prima facie case.
The renewed permission application was argued as a matter of principle about intervention before tribunal hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review after refusal on the papers.
enrichment.ratio: Save in exceptional circumstances where irreparable unfairness or injustice requires intervention, the court should not judicially review a disciplinary body's decision merely to refer allegations to a tribunal that will fully determine misconduct with the same sanctioning powers; procedural defects are ordinarily cured at tribunal level and merits are not for review at the referral stage.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review lies against a Law Society referral to the SDT
Effect of a subsequent prima facie case certification by the tribunal
Procedural fairness where disputed documents may not have been before the panel
Application of Morgan v Lloyd on premature intervention in disciplinary processes

enrichment.short_title: Estate agent commission after unauthorised sub-agent
key_facts: Mr Burney appointed London Mews as sole selling agent for Bryanston Mews West under a standard sole agency agreement.
London Mews sent particulars to Kaye & Co for circulation; Kaye & Co copied them, misrepresented itself to buyer Mr Cullinane, and refused to identify the vendor's agents.
Cullinane approached Burney directly and completed a private sale while Burney had told London Mews the property was off the market.
London Mews obtained default judgment for 2% plus VAT commission; Burney's application to set aside failed at two levels below.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court decision refusing to set aside default judgment for estate agent commission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; London Mews entitled to commission.
enrichment.ratio: Supplying particulars through another estate agent can amount to introducing the purchaser to the transaction where those particulars enable the buyer to approach the vendor directly; unauthorised officious conduct by a third agent does not break the chain of causation if the instructing agent lawfully provided the materials used, and McCann v Pow is distinguishable because London Mews relied on their own authorised acts rather than wrongful sub-agency.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'introduced by us' in a sole agency agreement
Whether Kaye & Co's unauthorised conduct broke the chain of causation
Distinction from McCann v Pow on unauthorised sub-agents
Construction of 'another agent' in the agency clause

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe robbery conviction after corrupt officers
key_facts: Thomas was convicted in 1994 of robbery and possessing a firearm with intent as look-out in a bookmakers raid based heavily on Rigg Approach Flying Squad officers.
Detective Constable Howell was later convicted of perverting the course of justice; Detective Sergeant Miller resigned after investigation; DC Smith was suspended.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case because the Crown case depended on officers no longer regarded as witnesses of truth.
The Crown conceded the 1994 conviction was unsafe; Thomas also appealed a later 2001 life sentence for a separate firearms offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal following CCRC reference against 1994 convictions; renewed sentence appeal against 2001 life sentence.
enrichment.outcome: 1994 convictions quashed; 2001 life sentence replaced with nine years' imprisonment; defendant's costs order granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a robbery conviction rests materially on evidence of police officers later shown to be corrupt or untrustworthy, and civilian evidence cannot sustain the verdict, the conviction is unsafe and must be quashed; time served on a quashed conviction does not give day-for-day credit against a later sentence for separate offences but may inform the appropriate determinate term.
legal_issues: Safety of conviction after corruption findings against key police witnesses
Impact of CCRC referral where Crown no longer supports conviction
Whether quashed 1994 conviction should reduce the 2001 life sentence
Disparity with co-defendant's 12-year sentence

confidence.notes: Conviction quashed by concession and sentence varied with explicit reasoning; outcomes are unambiguous.

enrichment.short_title: Civil liability for lifeboat launching gear breach
key_facts: A marine engineer was seriously injured when a port lifeboat suspension chain failed during a drill on the DSV Norlift at Teesport.
Failure was caused by stress corrosion cracking; negligence was not established but breach of reg 43(10) and Schedule 16 was admitted.
The judge held Todd v Adams prevented a civil claim because Merchant Shipping safety regulations did not confer private rights of action.
The Court of Appeal distinguished Todd, which concerned fishing vessel certification rules under section 121 rather than seafarers' life-saving regulations under section 85.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of a personal injury claim in the county court on breach of statutory duty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment for the claimant for damages to be assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Todd v Adams is binding on fishing vessel construction rules backed by a certification scheme under section 121 Merchant Shipping Act 1995, but does not extend to life-saving appliance regulations under section 85 intended to align seafarers' safety with terrestrial factory-style protection; breach of an absolute duty imposed for seamen's protection gives rise to a civil remedy despite general enforcement machinery.
legal_issues: Whether breach of Merchant Shipping (Life Saving Appliances) Regulations 1980 gives a private law cause of action
Distinction between Todd v Adams and Groves v Wimborne principles
Effect of criminal penalties and inspection regimes on civil liability
Applicability of regulation 53 where the ship was in port

enrichment.short_title: John Doe injunction over stolen Harry Potter manuscript
key_facts: Copies of Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix were stolen from secure printing before the June 2003 publication date.
The Sun published photographs of stolen proofs; a third party offered newspaper chapters for £25,000 each from a phone box.
The thief's identity was unknown, preventing conventional named-defendant relief.
Bloomsbury and JK Rowling sought injunctions against the person offering copies to newspapers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent without-notice interlocutory application in the Chancery Division for injunctive relief against unidentified defendants.
enrichment.outcome: John Doe injunction granted against the person or persons offering stolen copies to newspapers.
enrichment.ratio: Where wrongdoers can be identified by their acts rather than names and will understand an injunction directed at them, the court may grant effective injunctive relief against unnamed defendants; such orders bind the identified wrongdoer and those who knowingly assist dissemination once notified.

enrichment.short_title: Flooding nuisance trial wrongly cut short
key_facts: Baddeley and Allman's cottage at Linley Cottages flooded repeatedly from 1993 to 2000 from a pond on neighbour Barker's land after land drains were severed near a highway manhole.
Mr Willis carried out drainage works in February 1998 and inserted a temporary six-inch pipe in November 2000 after further floods.
Joint expert Mr Bate said only a culvert under the A5011 could fully solve drainage, but November 2000 works improved discharge from the pond.
The judge treated the trial as summary disposal on the expert report alone without hearing witness evidence on historical floods.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal at trial of nuisance and negligence claims for property flooding.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the county court for rehearing with early case management and mediation encouraged.
enrichment.ratio: A landowner must do what is reasonably possible to abate a nuisance emanating from their land, but liability for past flooding cannot be resolved by looking only at future abatement possibilities; where disputed facts concern the adequacy of earlier remedial works and causation of specific floods, summary disposal without evidence is unfair and the burden may shift under res ipsa loquitur once nuisance from the defendant's land is proved.
legal_issues: Extent of a landowner's duty to abate natural drainage nuisance under Leakey principles
Whether February 1998 and November 2000 drainage works abated or reduced the nuisance
Procedural fairness when a full trial is converted to summary judgment without notice
Burden of proof after nuisance from defendant's land is established
